summary: Defines a way to subscribe to a whole list of resources in SIP by putting the list inside the body of a single SUBSCRIBE request. Instead of one subscription per resource, the subscriber gets notifications about all of them through one dialog. This is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3265.

eli5.summary: Imagine ordering for a whole table by handing the waiter one list, instead of calling him over once for every dish. You ask once, and he keeps you posted on everything on the list.

subtitle: Subscribe to a whole list of SIP resources in one request by putting the list in the request body.

tldr.problem: Subscribing to many resources in SIP normally takes one SUBSCRIBE request per resource. RFC 4662 covers subscribing to an existing resource list but leaves list creation out of scope.
tldr.mechanism: The subscriber puts a flat list of URIs in the body of one SUBSCRIBE request and adds the 'recipient-list-subscribe' option-tag in a Require header field. The resource list server then reports on all the resources inside one dialog.
tldr.outcome: One dialog carries notifications for the whole list, and the server may offer a URI for managing the list. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3265.

facts.label: Reply to list in later SUBSCRIBE

today: RFC 5367 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It updates RFC 3265, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: One Request for a Whole List
sections.content:
RFC 4662 explains how to subscribe to a homogeneous list of resources in SIP and how to get notifications when those resources change. It does not say how the list gets created.

RFC 5367 fills that gap. A client creates a list and subscribes to it with a single SIP request, by placing the list of resources (as defined in RFC 5363) in the body of a SUBSCRIBE request. Without this, the subscriber would send one SUBSCRIBE per resource.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking about each friend one at a time, you give a single list and ask to be told when anything changes for anyone on it.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
A user agent client (UAC) builds a SUBSCRIBE request with at least one body whose disposition is type recipient-list, as defined in RFC 5363, containing the URI list. It MUST also put the recipient-list-subscribe option-tag in a Require header field, and build the rest of the request following RFC 3265.

The UAC MUST support the rlmi+xml format from RFC 4662 and signal it by listing rlmi+xml in the Accept header. It MAY support and list other formats.

The status code in the response says nothing about whether the server managed to subscribe to the URIs on the list. The client learns that from the notifications the server sends.

Once the dialog exists, the client can send subsequent SUBSCRIBE requests, for example to extend the subscription. Resource-list bodies have no meaning there, so UACs SHOULD NOT include them. The initial request goes to the public URI of the resource list, while later ones go to the URI the server provided when the dialog was established.
sections.eli5: You hand over your list and say you need special list service. The first answer only says 'got it'. The details about each person on the list arrive later in updates.

sections.title: The URI-List Document
sections.content:
RFC 5363 requires each URI-list service to name a default format for its list bodies. Here the default is the resource list format from RFC 4826. Clients that generate list bodies MUST support it, and so MUST resource list servers that handle them. Either side MAY support other formats.

That XCAP document format can express hierarchical lists and entries included by reference (<entry-ref>). This service only needs a flat list of URIs, so UAs SHOULD use flat lists and SHOULD NOT use <entry-ref> elements. A server that receives more than that MAY discard the extra information.

The RFC's example list contains three <entry> elements, each with a uri attribute such as sip:bill@example.com, inside a single <list>.
sections.eli5: The list is just a plain shopping list of addresses. No fancy folders inside folders, and no pointers to other lists.

sections.title: What the Resource List Server Does
sections.content:
A resource list server that can process a SUBSCRIBE with a recipient-list body SHOULD include the recipient-list-subscribe option-tag in a Supported header field when it answers OPTIONS requests. This lets clients discover the capability.

If the server chooses to accept the rlmi+xml format, it MUST comply with RFC 4662 for creating the subscription and for reporting changes to the resources inside the created dialog.

If a subsequent SUBSCRIBE carries a resource-list body, the server follows standard SIP procedures and rejects it with a 415 (Unsupported Media Type) response.

Managing the list

The server MAY give the client a URI for manipulating the list, using a Call-Info header field in the NOTIFY that establishes the subscription, with the purpose parameter set to list-management. The list lives only as long as the subscription: it SHOULD be destroyed when the subscription expires or ends. The RFC also updates the table in Section 7.1 of RFC 3265 so that Call-Info may optionally appear in NOTIFY requests.
sections.eli5: The waiter can say 'I can take list orders', and he looks after everything on your list. He may also give you a card to change the list. When your visit ends, the list is thrown away.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Servers that accept request-contained URI lists MUST follow the security guidance in RFC 4662. Because a resource list server that sends SUBSCRIBE requests to a set of users acts as a URI-list service, it MUST also follow the security rules in RFC 5363. Those rules include opt-in lists and mandatory authentication and authorization of clients.

IANA registered the list-management value for the purpose parameter of Call-Info, and the recipient-list-subscribe SIP option-tag. The option-tag is used to ensure that a server can process the recipient-list body used in a SUBSCRIBE request.
sections.eli5: Because the server will contact other people for you, it must check who you are and make sure those people agreed to be on lists.
